text:
239 of 653 Solana validators went the last three months without a single downtime incident.

The other 414 went offline at least once.

If you stake SOL, one of these validators is holding it. Most people have no idea which group theirs is in, because downtime is quiet.

What downtime looks like

A validator can stop voting. Voting is how it confirms blocks, and Solana pays staking rewards for every vote that lands on time. When your validator goes silent, your rewards stop too. Nothing gets slashed and your APY barely moves, so you end up with a little less SOL and no idea why.

It can also stop producing blocks. Every validator gets turns to make blocks, based on how much stake it holds. A node that's down or slow leaves those turns empty, and the fees and tips from those blocks never reach you. It can keep voting the whole time, so most dashboards still show it as healthy.

What it cost

Between them, Solana validators spent about 4,200 hours offline since the start of July. Stakers missed roughly 3,400 SOL in rewards, and that only counts missed votes.

Plenty of big names were on the list:

@binance: 5.4 hours offline, 185 SOL lost by its stakers
@P2Pvalidator: 8.4 hours across 8 nodes, 89 SOL
@Helius: 2.5 hours, 77 SOL
@everstake_pool: under 2 hours, 71 SOL
@coinbase: 9.8 hours across 18 nodes, 28 SOL

On August 12 one hosting provider had a routing failure and 167 validators went dark at once. Stakers lost 224 SOL in about half an hour.

Who got paid back
About 64 SOL of the total sat on stake delegated through Marinade. When a Marinade validator goes down, the validator pays Marinade stakers back.

The other 3,357 SOL belonged to everyone else. Nobody paid it back.

Explore

We built Explore so you can check this for any validator on Solana. Every incident shows how long it lasted, how much SOL stakers missed, and whether anyone covered it.

Look up yours at https://t.co/Zf5mzHzE9g

They worked there so late, so often, that anyone who got locked out at night knew to call one of them (e.g. @charliecurnin who doubled as their engineering recruiter)

Before Listen, Alfred and Florian built a consumer app called BeFake that went viral and got 20,000 users overnight. It also had a churn problem. To understand why people were leaving, they built an AI that could interview their users for them (a challenge @schreier knew immensely well). That tool became the company.

They saw that most product decisions get made without customer input, because talking to customers is slow and expensive. A meaningful market research study could take a year.

@Listen made research continuous, with AI running the interviews and synthesizing the answers, so a company could hear from its customers every week.
Sequoia had the privilege of leading their seed round in 2023, before they even had a demo, because Bryan, Charlie, Jess and our team believed in the two of them. Bryan went on to be their steadfast product partner and founder coach for years.

A great idea only gets you so far. Alfred and Florian are exceptional builders, and they attracted a team just as strong. That team did the hard work of turning an idea into a product that marketers love.

They showed their craftsmanship up close because Sequoia was one of Listen's first customers. The product spread through our firm on its own, and we used it for everything from peer feedback to diligence on potential partnerships.

By the time Sequoia led their Series A, we had looked at every similar product on the market, and Listen was still the clear standout. About a year after launch, they were serving 20% of the Fortune 500.

Alfred likes to say that as AI makes building easier, the hard part becomes knowing what to build.

Listen helps companies answer that by talking to their customers, and with Salesforce, every company can do the same.

Congratulations and thank you to my friends Alfred, Florian and the entire Listen Labs team, and to @Marc Benioff and the Salesforce team. This is the start of something special.

1) AI is a field of computer science dating back half a century. that doesn't magically get undone via presidential mandate

2) the flows around AI are more largely explained by the size of the tokens. it is much easier (cheaper) to push a token from 7 fig to 8 fig where all participants are happy to realize a multiple than it is from low 9 fig to high 9 fig / 10 fig.

2026 年 9 月 29 日，OpenAI 在旧金山 Fort Mason 办了今年的开发者大会 DevDay。主讲是 CEO Sam Altman。其他几位上台的人都在做这些产品。产品团队的 Holly 演示了新产品 Dots。后训练（模型预训练之后做对齐和能力调优的阶段）研究负责人 Tejal 讲了模型怎么反过来帮 OpenAI 做研究。Codex 的演示由 Romain Huet 来做，他在 OpenAI 负责开发者体验，去年 DevDay 主题演讲里的 Codex 演示也是他做的。整场演讲分三块：面向用户的常驻智能体 Dots 和协作空间 ChatGPT Space，给开发者的新模型和新工具，以及帮开发者做分发、赚钱的渠道。

1. Dots：一直在线、会主动干活的智能体

Sam 把 Dots 比作电影里那种一直在身边帮忙的 AI 助手。他认为订餐厅、买机票这类代办虽然有用，但和这项技术能做的事比起来太小了。他想要的 AI 知道正在发生什么，也知道你在意什么，不用你事事交代。

Dots 是常驻在线的智能体（Agent），有自己的云端电脑和浏览器，能写代码、跑测试。它的权限跟着用户走，能直接用用户已经在 ChatGPT 里连好的插件，覆盖 4000 多个应用。除了在 ChatGPT 里对话，之后还可以给它发短信、打电话。目前每人先有一个 Dot，以后可以配一整组。Dots 跑在 本月早些时候发布的 GPT-6 Astra 上，Sam 称它是 OpenAI 对齐做得最好的模型。用户可以限定 Dot 能用哪些应用、能不能操作电脑，也能给它的各类操作写自定义指令，愿意交出多少责任就放多少权。

Sam 说，他自己的 Dot 每天早上会把夜里进来的消息过一遍，挑出紧急的提醒他。他说这让他拿回了一部分注意力，没那么离不开手机了。他还举了一个更重的例子：把应用从一个即将停用的旧 API 上迁走。这个 API 可能散落在代码库各处，改了哪里会连带弄坏什么，事先看不出来。Dot 可以追踪依赖关系，找出所有要改的地方，写代码、跑测试，最后把 PR（代码合并请求）交给团队审。他让听众想想，过去做这件事要几个人、花多久。

开场视频里，用户把自己的 Dot 改名叫 Alfred。Alfred 和另一个 Dot 帮用户上线网站，改董事会材料，在婚礼蛋糕商家取消后找好备选。它们还发现财务会和女儿的演出撞了期，提出改时间。每件事都是 Dot 推进到需要人确认的地方，再由人拍板。

2. ChatGPT Space：人和智能体一起用的工作区

Sam 认为，现有的生产力软件几乎都没考虑过人和 AI 一起干活。ChatGPT Space 以页面为单位，可以在里面写计划、做调研、生成图片和数据。页面和文件像网盘一样放在同一个空间里。Dot 能直接在页面上工作，在评论里 @ 它，它就会接活。页面本身也能带指令，比如“每天去看 API 平台的 Slack 频道，把发现更新到这里”。之后 Space 里还会加入演示文稿，格式做成智能体方便读写的样子，团队成员可以和各自的 Dot 一起改。

在 Holly 的演示里，页面用斜杠命令就能插入交互图表、表格和可运行的原型。她 @ 自己的 Dot（名叫 Dotty），让它把一组数据改成柱状图。图表可以按反馈类型筛选，Dotty 每小时刷新一次。她还让 Dotty 把“某位工程师在我 Slack 私信里提过的新手引导数据”补进 FAQ。Dotty 能看到她的上下文，所以这种模糊的指代也找得到。

3. OpenAI 内部怎么用 Dots

Holly 用一个虚构的歌单应用 Blossom Music，模拟发布前一天的状况。早上 Dotty 已经做了几件事：发现发布评审会提前，改好了日历；看完前一晚测试用户的反馈；注意到设计团队临时改了首页，把新设计发给她。她让 Dotty 直接把这个设计做出来。Dotty 调用她笔记本上的 Codex 构建应用，在 iPhone 模拟器里跑起来，再提交 PR。现场的语音演示卡住了，Dotty 一直回复“还在查”。Codex 线程也报过一次错，她重试后才继续下去。

她说，Dots 真正改变 OpenAI 工作方式的地方在 Slack。Dots 在公司 Slack 里有自己的身份，员工就开始把它们当作代理人。被同事 @ 到的零碎请求，直接转给自己的 Dot 处理。建群时，大家从一开始就把各自的 Dot 拉进来，Dot 带回结果时所有人都能看到。

工程师走得更远。有人在反馈频道贴出会话 ID 和一个用户 bug，某位工程师的 Dot 就会接手排查，提 PR 修复。她说这是真实情况：工程师们的 Dots 每天这样修掉几十个 bug，Dots 这个产品本身有很多部分就是 Dots 写的。

4. 上线范围和企业用的 Specialist Dots

Dots 和 Space 当天向 ChatGPT Pro、Business Premium 和 Enterprise 用户开放。Dot 包含在套餐里，和它的对话不占用额度。

企业客户还可以预览 Specialist Dots。这是由公司统一设置、供整个团队使用的虚拟同事，负责会计、市场、法务这类工作量大的事。公司给它目标和背景，审核它的产出，给它反馈，反馈在全公司共享。OpenAI 也在和微软合作，把 Specialist Dots 接入 Agent 365（微软用来管理企业智能体的工具），企业可以用已经在用的微软工具来管理它们。

5. 新模型：更便宜的 GPT-6.1 Sol，更快的 UltraFast

Astra 发布这几周，用户的要求集中在两点：更便宜，更快。GPT-6.1 Sol（转录稿误作 Soul）的能力接近 Astra，价格是它的五分之一。缓存输入（重复发送、已被缓存的上下文）比标准输入便宜 95%。智能体需要反复读同一批上下文、长时间迭代，这对它们尤其省钱。Sam 说 Sol 在某些方面比 Astra 还聪明，定位是开发者的日常主力模型。

UltraFast 是新的速度档，API、ChatGPT 和 Codex 里都能用。原有的 Fast 档是两倍速度、两倍价格；UltraFast 是八倍速度、六倍价格，每秒 300 个 Token。它现在可以配合 Astra 用，之后也会支持 Sol。现场让两个模型用同一个提示词，做一个 DevDay 配色的火箭。UltraFast 的火箭已经升空时，标准速度的还没做完。

订阅也跟着调整。新推出的 500 美元档 Pro 订阅叫 Pro 500，额度最高，是 Plus 的 25 倍。它可以在 ChatGPT 和 Codex 里用 UltraFast，还能通过“用 ChatGPT 登录”在合作方的应用里使用。Pro 200 重新开放，继续提供所有前沿模型。

另外预览了 Decisions API。它给 Luna 模型一组预先定义好的选项，让模型从中选一个，比如给请求分流、给图片分类、决定智能体下一步做什么。任务收窄成选择题之后，响应时间可以压到一秒以内，同时保留图像理解、多语言和安全防护。Romain 后来补充说，做机器人的朋友看中的是它能处理视觉输入：机器人可以根据看到的东西，近乎实时地快速行动。

6. 模型开始帮 OpenAI 做研究

Sam 提到，去年这个时候，他和 Jakob 在一次直播里预测，一年内会出现第一个“AI 研究实习生”，当时几乎没人相信。几周前 OpenAI 宣布达成了这个目标：有了一个能接手定义清晰的研究任务的系统，这类任务原本要熟练的研究员花大量时间和精力。

Tejal 的方向是电脑操作（computer use，让模型像人一样操作桌面和浏览器）。她举了两个例子。

第一个是让模型优化电脑操作的运行框架（harness，包在模型外面、负责调用工具和管理步骤的代码）。模型在循环里持续寻找能同时降低延迟、提升效果的改动，团队把找到的改进合进生产环境的框架，并用于后训练。结果是延迟改善了两倍以上，已经上线。

第二个是模型帮忙改进了监控和拒绝训练，让 Astra 在不安全的场景里更会拒绝。Astra 在电脑操作压力测试上因此达到业内领先，操作时出错更少，也更贴合用户的本意。

她给出了几项内部数据。今年夏天之后，研究工作消耗的 Token 量急剧上升。1 月时，模型能做好 15 分钟以内的短任务，需要一天以上的任务大多会失败；到 7 月，超过三分之一的一天量级研究任务，模型能在无人干预下完成。她还提到，Astra 这类模型已经帮忙解决了 100 多个悬而未决几十年的数学问题，也在参与针对耐药感染的新抗生素、古代语言研究、可再生能源和工业机器人等方向的工作。

7. 给开发者的底层工具

Sam 说，OpenAI 想让开发者用上自己内部用的东西。

第一件是 Codex 的运行框架。它同时支撑着 Codex、ChatGPT Work 和 Dots，目标是用最少的 Token、最快拿到准确结果，现在已经开源。第二件是 Codex 完全上云：在手机上开始的任务，可以在浏览器或桌面端接着做，合上笔记本任务也不会中断。

云端能力带来了 Codex Security Cloud。它在云端环境里持续寻找漏洞，并准备好验证过的修复方案供人审核，这次新增了自动去重、定时扫描和新界面。Sam 说这是为了给防守方更好的工具，因为“我们看得到接下来会发生什么”。

新的 Agents API 进入公开测试。它包含运行框架、托管、记忆、多智能体控制等功能，是 Codex 和 Dots 用的同一套技术，也加入了电脑操作能力。现场的例子是一个网站测试智能体，会自己打开浏览器、点击页面、测试流程。基础设施方面，OpenAI 和 AWS 合作推出由 OpenAI 驱动的 Bedrock（AWS 的托管 AI 服务）托管智能体，AWS 客户可以直接使用 OpenAI 的前沿模型、Codex 和 ChatGPT Work。

隐私方面预览了 OpenAI Private Intelligence。其中的零数据留存（ZDR）配合私有安全处理，可以在不把用户内容存到 OpenAI 服务器的情况下做安全检测；私有推理则把隐私保护延伸到推理阶段。Sam 说这套方案是和最大的一批客户一起设计的，目的是让他们能把模型用在最敏感的工作上。

性能方面，Responses API 一年里增长了 100 倍，可靠性保持在 99% 以上。首个 Token 的等待时间缩短了 45%，工具调用和工作流提速 30% 以上。

8. Romain 的 Codex 演示

演示从手机上的 Codex 开始。Romain 人还在会场外，让 Codex 替他跟观众打招呼、讲一个会场的冷知识。接着他用几张会场照片生成的 3D 场景演示 UltraFast，一边说一边改：把小人放到座位上，把直播画面投到场景里的大屏幕上。现场语音没连上，他改成了打字。

Codex 命令行工具（CLI）这次全面翻新。他让 UltraFast 写一个应用，从观众里随机抽三个人送明年的门票，几秒就写完；改成抽六个人，也几乎是瞬间完成。命令行现在支持由 GPT Live 驱动的双向实时语音，不只是语音转文字，但现场没能演示出来。

后面几段演示了多模态和电脑操作。游戏 Astra Adventures 从一张纸上的草图开始，几轮之后画面还很粗糙，借助图像模型，才变成有质感、能用在正式游戏里的美术。然后他让 Astra 通过浏览器自己学着玩这个游戏，屏幕左边显示模型的决策，右边显示它按下的按键。

他又用“应用快照”（app shot）把自己记录飞行课程的应用作为上下文交给 Codex，让它在各种屏幕尺寸下审查这个应用并截图。Codex 自己在模拟器里点开了各项功能。云端 Codex 现在和本地版用同样的工具，包括插件和电脑操作。他顺手把一个“用 Rust 重写整个后端”的任务丢到云端，打算稍后在手机上查看。

最后一个演示用的是 Hugging Face 借来的可编程小机器人 Micro Duck，它名叫 Lavender。Romain 前一晚让 Codex 把它接好：视觉用 Astra，图像生成用 GPT Image 2.5，语音交互用 GPT Live 1。机器人现场看着观众画了一幅画。他说，OpenAI 做 Dots 和 Codex 用的，就是 API 里开放给开发者的同一批工具。

9. 分发和变现：让开发者在 ChatGPT 上做生意

ChatGPT 每周大约有 12 亿人使用。Sam 承认，此前类似的尝试效果参差不齐。他说这次有信心，是因为开发者拿到的是 OpenAI 自己做 ChatGPT 用的工具。

第一项是“用 ChatGPT 登录”（Sign in with ChatGPT）。用户登录第三方应用时，可以直接用自己 ChatGPT 套餐里包含的 Token，开发者不必替新用户垫付模型费用。首批有 16 家合作方。

第二项是插件扩展（plugin extensions）。开发者可以把编辑器、仪表盘乃至整个工作区，做成原生嵌在 ChatGPT 和 Codex 里的应用。现场展示了三个例子。一个是会议应用：在 ChatGPT 里看日历上的会议，点“记笔记”后，页面变成团队和 Dots 一起跟进待办的 Space。一个是 Figma：打开设计稿、看团队评论、让 ChatGPT 改稿。还有一个是 Adobe：在 ChatGPT 里使用 Photoshop 的功能。ChatGPT sites（在 ChatGPT 里生成的网站，几个月里已有数百万个）现在也能接入插件和数据。访客用自己的账号登录、带上自己的智能体，看到的内容因人而异。

用户发现插件的渠道也扩大了。除了在插件库里搜索，ChatGPT 还会在对话中识别出能帮上忙的插件，用户当场就能连接。插件审核流程也简化了：开发者可以跟踪审核进度，看到需要修改的地方，申请人工复审，更新工具时也不用从头提交。

第三项是 OpenAI Marketplace，首批有 30 多家合作方，包括 CodeRabbit、Notion、Vercel。企业客户可以用已经和 OpenAI 签下的采购承诺额度来买这些产品，有承诺额度的开发者也能在这里花。通过和模型推理托管公司 Baseten（转录稿写作 Base10）合作，市场里还能用到开源模型。

10. 收尾：一次额度重置，和“文艺复兴”的说法

当天的后续安排里，Peter 会讲 OpenAI 对开源社区的投入，包括新的 OpenClaw Enterprise Harness（OpenClaw 是一个开源 AI 智能体项目）。还有一个 Codex 游戏工作室环节，观众可以用 Codex 做复古游戏，每人能领一台 DevDay 限定的 chromatic computer，用来玩自己做的游戏。最后是 Sam、Tibo (Thibault) 和 Tejal 的现场问答。

Sam 和 Tibo 还在台上按下按钮，给全世界的用户重置了一次用量额度。Sam 说 OpenAI 已经做过太多次重置，Tibo 一直想把公司改名叫“重置公司”。

最后 Sam 说，他不喜欢把 AI 比作新一轮工业革命，那意味着人变成巨大机器里的齿轮，转得越来越快；生活里有些部分不能也不该被自动化。他希望，如果做对了，AI 带来的会更像一场新的文艺复兴：让人对自己的生活有更多掌控，有更多工具去创造、学习和探索。

text:
Websites are starting to publish the tools an agent can call instead of making the agent click around like a confused human.

@OpenAIDevs just announced the winners of its WebMCP Challenge. The idea is simple: a website exposes structured actions, and people and agents use the same live service.

That moves leverage from the model alone to the business that defines the allowed actions. A bank, travel site or retailer with better tools can become easier for an agent to use than a competitor with a prettier interface.

Agents still need models. But the companies that control the rails those models use to search, buy and execute will own a much bigger part of the relationship.

The web is being rebuilt as a set of callable services. That is a much bigger change than adding a chatbot to a page.

text:
Every era of markets answered one question differently: who gets to see your intent before you trade  

Open outcry. Traders in a pit, shouting and signalling. Your plan stayed in your head until you opened your mouth, then the whole pit heard it and got in ahead of you  

Electronic. Screens and matching engines. The crowd sees your orders but not your name, and your stops sit on the exchange's server. You trust the venue with everything  

Onchain. No venue to trust, but now everyone sees everything. Every order, stop and position tied to a wallet, readable by anyone, including the bots paid to trade against them  

Encrypted. Still no venue to trust, but now nobody sees anything. Your instruction stays sealed until its condition is met, then it fires and settles like any other trade, and not even the network reads it in between  

That's covenants. Mainnet is first week of October

text:
2026 年 9 月 29 日，OpenAI 在旧金山 Fort Mason 办了今年的开发者大会 DevDay。主讲是 CEO Sam Altman。其他几位上台的人都在做这些产品。产品团队的 Holly 演示了新产品 Dots。后训练（模型预训练之后做对齐和能力调优的阶段）研究负责人 Tejal 讲了模型怎么反过来帮 OpenAI 做研究。Codex 的演示由 Romain Huet 来做，他在 OpenAI 负责开发者体验，去年 DevDay 主题演讲里的 Codex 演示也是他做的。整场演讲分三块：面向用户的常驻智能体 Dots 和协作空间 ChatGPT Space，给开发者的新模型和新工具，以及帮开发者做分发、赚钱的渠道。

1. Dots：一直在线、会主动干活的智能体

Sam 把 Dots 比作电影里那种一直在身边帮忙的 AI 助手。他认为订餐厅、买机票这类代办虽然有用，但和这项技术能做的事比起来太小了。他想要的 AI 知道正在发生什么，也知道你在意什么，不用你事事交代。

Dots 是常驻在线的智能体（Agent），有自己的云端电脑和浏览器，能写代码、跑测试。它的权限跟着用户走，能直接用用户已经在 ChatGPT 里连好的插件，覆盖 4000 多个应用。除了在 ChatGPT 里对话，之后还可以给它发短信、打电话。目前每人先有一个 Dot，以后可以配一整组。Dots 跑在 本月早些时候发布的 GPT-6 Astra 上，Sam 称它是 OpenAI 对齐做得最好的模型。用户可以限定 Dot 能用哪些应用、能不能操作电脑，也能给它的各类操作写自定义指令，愿意交出多少责任就放多少权。

Sam 说，他自己的 Dot 每天早上会把夜里进来的消息过一遍，挑出紧急的提醒他。他说这让他拿回了一部分注意力，没那么离不开手机了。他还举了一个更重的例子：把应用从一个即将停用的旧 API 上迁走。这个 API 可能散落在代码库各处，改了哪里会连带弄坏什么，事先看不出来。Dot 可以追踪依赖关系，找出所有要改的地方，写代码、跑测试，最后把 PR（代码合并请求）交给团队审。他让听众想想，过去做这件事要几个人、花多久。

开场视频里，用户把自己的 Dot 改名叫 Alfred。Alfred 和另一个 Dot 帮用户上线网站，改董事会材料，在婚礼蛋糕商家取消后找好备选。它们还发现财务会和女儿的演出撞了期，提出改时间。每件事都是 Dot 推进到需要人确认的地方，再由人拍板。

2. ChatGPT Space：人和智能体一起用的工作区

Sam 认为，现有的生产力软件几乎都没考虑过人和 AI 一起干活。ChatGPT Space 以页面为单位，可以在里面写计划、做调研、生成图片和数据。页面和文件像网盘一样放在同一个空间里。Dot 能直接在页面上工作，在评论里 @ 它，它就会接活。页面本身也能带指令，比如“每天去看 API 平台的 Slack 频道，把发现更新到这里”。之后 Space 里还会加入演示文稿，格式做成智能体方便读写的样子，团队成员可以和各自的 Dot 一起改。

在 Holly 的演示里，页面用斜杠命令就能插入交互图表、表格和可运行的原型。她 @ 自己的 Dot（名叫 Dotty），让它把一组数据改成柱状图。图表可以按反馈类型筛选，Dotty 每小时刷新一次。她还让 Dotty 把“某位工程师在我 Slack 私信里提过的新手引导数据”补进 FAQ。Dotty 能看到她的上下文，所以这种模糊的指代也找得到。

3. OpenAI 内部怎么用 Dots

Holly 用一个虚构的歌单应用 Blossom Music，模拟发布前一天的状况。早上 Dotty 已经做了几件事：发现发布评审会提前，改好了日历；看完前一晚测试用户的反馈；注意到设计团队临时改了首页，把新设计发给她。她让 Dotty 直接把这个设计做出来。Dotty 调用她笔记本上的 Codex 构建应用，在 iPhone 模拟器里跑起来，再提交 PR。现场的语音演示卡住了，Dotty 一直回复“还在查”。Codex 线程也报过一次错，她重试后才继续下去。

她说，Dots 真正改变 OpenAI 工作方式的地方在 Slack。Dots 在公司 Slack 里有自己的身份，员工就开始把它们当作代理人。被同事 @ 到的零碎请求，直接转给自己的 Dot 处理。建群时，大家从一开始就把各自的 Dot 拉进来，Dot 带回结果时所有人都能看到。

工程师走得更远。有人在反馈频道贴出会话 ID 和一个用户 bug，某位工程师的 Dot 就会接手排查，提 PR 修复。她说这是真实情况：工程师们的 Dots 每天这样修掉几十个 bug，Dots 这个产品本身有很多部分就是 Dots 写的。

4. 上线范围和企业用的 Specialist Dots

Dots 和 Space 当天向 ChatGPT Pro、Business Premium 和 Enterprise 用户开放。Dot 包含在套餐里，和它的对话不占用额度。

企业客户还可以预览 Specialist Dots。这是由公司统一设置、供整个团队使用的虚拟同事，负责会计、市场、法务这类工作量大的事。公司给它目标和背景，审核它的产出，给它反馈，反馈在全公司共享。OpenAI 也在和微软合作，把 Specialist Dots 接入 Agent 365（微软用来管理企业智能体的工具），企业可以用已经在用的微软工具来管理它们。

5. 新模型：更便宜的 GPT-6.1 Sol，更快的 UltraFast

Astra 发布这几周，用户的要求集中在两点：更便宜，更快。GPT-6.1 Sol（转录稿误作 Soul）的能力接近 Astra，价格是它的五分之一。缓存输入（重复发送、已被缓存的上下文）比标准输入便宜 95%。智能体需要反复读同一批上下文、长时间迭代，这对它们尤其省钱。Sam 说 Sol 在某些方面比 Astra 还聪明，定位是开发者的日常主力模型。

UltraFast 是新的速度档，API、ChatGPT 和 Codex 里都能用。原有的 Fast 档是两倍速度、两倍价格；UltraFast 是八倍速度、六倍价格，每秒 300 个 Token。它现在可以配合 Astra 用，之后也会支持 Sol。现场让两个模型用同一个提示词，做一个 DevDay 配色的火箭。UltraFast 的火箭已经升空时，标准速度的还没做完。

订阅也跟着调整。新推出的 500 美元档 Pro 订阅叫 Pro 500，额度最高，是 Plus 的 25 倍。它可以在 ChatGPT 和 Codex 里用 UltraFast，还能通过“用 ChatGPT 登录”在合作方的应用里使用。Pro 200 重新开放，继续提供所有前沿模型。

另外预览了 Decisions API。它给 Luna 模型一组预先定义好的选项，让模型从中选一个，比如给请求分流、给图片分类、决定智能体下一步做什么。任务收窄成选择题之后，响应时间可以压到一秒以内，同时保留图像理解、多语言和安全防护。Romain 后来补充说，做机器人的朋友看中的是它能处理视觉输入：机器人可以根据看到的东西，近乎实时地快速行动。

6. 模型开始帮 OpenAI 做研究

Sam 提到，去年这个时候，他和 Jakob 在一次直播里预测，一年内会出现第一个“AI 研究实习生”，当时几乎没人相信。几周前 OpenAI 宣布达成了这个目标：有了一个能接手定义清晰的研究任务的系统，这类任务原本要熟练的研究员花大量时间和精力。

Tejal 的方向是电脑操作（computer use，让模型像人一样操作桌面和浏览器）。她举了两个例子。

第一个是让模型优化电脑操作的运行框架（harness，包在模型外面、负责调用工具和管理步骤的代码）。模型在循环里持续寻找能同时降低延迟、提升效果的改动，团队把找到的改进合进生产环境的框架，并用于后训练。结果是延迟改善了两倍以上，已经上线。

第二个是模型帮忙改进了监控和拒绝训练，让 Astra 在不安全的场景里更会拒绝。Astra 在电脑操作压力测试上因此达到业内领先，操作时出错更少，也更贴合用户的本意。

她给出了几项内部数据。今年夏天之后，研究工作消耗的 Token 量急剧上升。1 月时，模型能做好 15 分钟以内的短任务，需要一天以上的任务大多会失败；到 7 月，超过三分之一的一天量级研究任务，模型能在无人干预下完成。她还提到，Astra 这类模型已经帮忙解决了 100 多个悬而未决几十年的数学问题，也在参与针对耐药感染的新抗生素、古代语言研究、可再生能源和工业机器人等方向的工作。

7. 给开发者的底层工具

Sam 说，OpenAI 想让开发者用上自己内部用的东西。

第一件是 Codex 的运行框架。它同时支撑着 Codex、ChatGPT Work 和 Dots，目标是用最少的 Token、最快拿到准确结果，现在已经开源。第二件是 Codex 完全上云：在手机上开始的任务，可以在浏览器或桌面端接着做，合上笔记本任务也不会中断。

云端能力带来了 Codex Security Cloud。它在云端环境里持续寻找漏洞，并准备好验证过的修复方案供人审核，这次新增了自动去重、定时扫描和新界面。Sam 说这是为了给防守方更好的工具，因为“我们看得到接下来会发生什么”。

新的 Agents API 进入公开测试。它包含运行框架、托管、记忆、多智能体控制等功能，是 Codex 和 Dots 用的同一套技术，也加入了电脑操作能力。现场的例子是一个网站测试智能体，会自己打开浏览器、点击页面、测试流程。基础设施方面，OpenAI 和 AWS 合作推出由 OpenAI 驱动的 Bedrock（AWS 的托管 AI 服务）托管智能体，AWS 客户可以直接使用 OpenAI 的前沿模型、Codex 和 ChatGPT Work。

隐私方面预览了 OpenAI Private Intelligence。其中的零数据留存（ZDR）配合私有安全处理，可以在不把用户内容存到 OpenAI 服务器的情况下做安全检测；私有推理则把隐私保护延伸到推理阶段。Sam 说这套方案是和最大的一批客户一起设计的，目的是让他们能把模型用在最敏感的工作上。

性能方面，Responses API 一年里增长了 100 倍，可靠性保持在 99% 以上。首个 Token 的等待时间缩短了 45%，工具调用和工作流提速 30% 以上。

8. Romain 的 Codex 演示

演示从手机上的 Codex 开始。Romain 人还在会场外，让 Codex 替他跟观众打招呼、讲一个会场的冷知识。接着他用几张会场照片生成的 3D 场景演示 UltraFast，一边说一边改：把小人放到座位上，把直播画面投到场景里的大屏幕上。现场语音没连上，他改成了打字。

Codex 命令行工具（CLI）这次全面翻新。他让 UltraFast 写一个应用，从观众里随机抽三个人送明年的门票，几秒就写完；改成抽六个人，也几乎是瞬间完成。命令行现在支持由 GPT Live 驱动的双向实时语音，不只是语音转文字，但现场没能演示出来。

后面几段演示了多模态和电脑操作。游戏 Astra Adventures 从一张纸上的草图开始，几轮之后画面还很粗糙，借助图像模型，才变成有质感、能用在正式游戏里的美术。然后他让 Astra 通过浏览器自己学着玩这个游戏，屏幕左边显示模型的决策，右边显示它按下的按键。

他又用“应用快照”（app shot）把自己记录飞行课程的应用作为上下文交给 Codex，让它在各种屏幕尺寸下审查这个应用并截图。Codex 自己在模拟器里点开了各项功能。云端 Codex 现在和本地版用同样的工具，包括插件和电脑操作。他顺手把一个“用 Rust 重写整个后端”的任务丢到云端，打算稍后在手机上查看。

最后一个演示用的是 Hugging Face 借来的可编程小机器人 Micro Duck，它名叫 Lavender。Romain 前一晚让 Codex 把它接好：视觉用 Astra，图像生成用 GPT Image 2.5，语音交互用 GPT Live 1。机器人现场看着观众画了一幅画。他说，OpenAI 做 Dots 和 Codex 用的，就是 API 里开放给开发者的同一批工具。

9. 分发和变现：让开发者在 ChatGPT 上做生意

ChatGPT 每周大约有 12 亿人使用。Sam 承认，此前类似的尝试效果参差不齐。他说这次有信心，是因为开发者拿到的是 OpenAI 自己做 ChatGPT 用的工具。

第一项是“用 ChatGPT 登录”（Sign in with ChatGPT）。用户登录第三方应用时，可以直接用自己 ChatGPT 套餐里包含的 Token，开发者不必替新用户垫付模型费用。首批有 16 家合作方。

第二项是插件扩展（plugin extensions）。开发者可以把编辑器、仪表盘乃至整个工作区，做成原生嵌在 ChatGPT 和 Codex 里的应用。现场展示了三个例子。一个是会议应用：在 ChatGPT 里看日历上的会议，点“记笔记”后，页面变成团队和 Dots 一起跟进待办的 Space。一个是 Figma：打开设计稿、看团队评论、让 ChatGPT 改稿。还有一个是 Adobe：在 ChatGPT 里使用 Photoshop 的功能。ChatGPT sites（在 ChatGPT 里生成的网站，几个月里已有数百万个）现在也能接入插件和数据。访客用自己的账号登录、带上自己的智能体，看到的内容因人而异。

用户发现插件的渠道也扩大了。除了在插件库里搜索，ChatGPT 还会在对话中识别出能帮上忙的插件，用户当场就能连接。插件审核流程也简化了：开发者可以跟踪审核进度，看到需要修改的地方，申请人工复审，更新工具时也不用从头提交。

第三项是 OpenAI Marketplace，首批有 30 多家合作方，包括 CodeRabbit、Notion、Vercel。企业客户可以用已经和 OpenAI 签下的采购承诺额度来买这些产品，有承诺额度的开发者也能在这里花。通过和模型推理托管公司 Baseten（转录稿写作 Base10）合作，市场里还能用到开源模型。

10. 收尾：一次额度重置，和“文艺复兴”的说法

当天的后续安排里，Peter 会讲 OpenAI 对开源社区的投入，包括新的 OpenClaw Enterprise Harness（OpenClaw 是一个开源 AI 智能体项目）。还有一个 Codex 游戏工作室环节，观众可以用 Codex 做复古游戏，每人能领一台 DevDay 限定的 chromatic computer，用来玩自己做的游戏。最后是 Sam、Tibo (Thibault) 和 Tejal 的现场问答。

Sam 和 Tibo 还在台上按下按钮，给全世界的用户重置了一次用量额度。Sam 说 OpenAI 已经做过太多次重置，Tibo 一直想把公司改名叫“重置公司”。

author: vincentweisser
quoted_text:
Some personal news: I'm joining @PrimeIntellect as Head of Scientific AI!

A billion copies of the same very smart, agreeable mind will not be a scientifically fruitful world.

Scientific superintelligence should be weird and definitionally nonconsensus. It should be highly plural, consisting of many minds, human and artificial, that see the world differently and hold each other accountable, with human judgement still playing the central role in setting the trajectory.

Science is about asking the right questions and reducing uncertainty. Professionalizing science made discovery a viable career, but it also introduced incentives to work on what is fundable and publishable. Neither is the same thing as being true or impactful (reward hacking exists in the real world too!). We are very good at accumulating incremental knowledge and rather bad at stewarding unorthodox ideas through infancy, even though these are often the ideas that open entirely new fields of inquiry.

If we aren't careful, scientific AI could reproduce these same incentives at a much larger scale. If everyone relies on the same few large models, we risk inheriting the same priors and blind spots.

Open tools let us shape our own intelligence and take it in directions a frontier lab might never prioritize. This matters for scientific freedom and is central to Prime’s vision.

If you are a scientist, staying at the frontier will mean training your own models on your own research and data. I'll work closely with scientific teams across domains to help them build scientific agents by turning their research problems into environments where agents can learn. This means closing the loop from hypothesis to experiment to validated result, with agents learning from each cycle. Teams will be able to own their intelligence, using tools previously available only to frontier labs, and point it at the questions they care about most, especially those that others might not be asking.

I've had the good fortune of seeing how science operates across academia, industry, government, startups, and venture. I worked on experimental therapeutics for cancer in academia before moving to the National Institutes of Health to work on DNA damage and repair. I cofounded Molecule, where we funded dozens of research projects to speed the translation of early-stage therapeutics to market, focusing on areas traditionally ignored by pharma. Most recently, I started Triplicate, a small fund backing teams and tools accelerating scientific research. Many of the problems I care about most are increasingly soluble with advances in AI, and I hope to bring what I've learned about the bottlenecks in translating research to radically accelerate science in all fields.

I share Alexander Grothendieck's ethos of discovery and believe Prime does too: "Discovery is a child's privilege. I mean the small child, the child who is not afraid to be wrong, to look silly, to not be serious, and to act differently from everyone else."

The goal of progress is not more intelligence for its own sake. In my view, it is to better understand reality, and, in doing so, give more people, and more kinds of minds, the chance to flourish.

If you have a research problem where today's tools fall short, my DMs are open. If our approach resonates and you want to build this with us, we're hiring!

Last week, @htaneja joined @hirshjain at our office for a fireside chat on the state of AI and venture.

Hemant talked about the moment ChatGPT launched. It was the first time a single technology had every CEO, in every industry, in every country, grappling to figure out what to do with it.

For General Catalyst, that came with a recognition: the world was going to be transformed, and the real question was what role to play in that transformation. 

The principle of "inclusive prosperity," where you empower everyone to do the transforming themselves, ties closely to Percepta's mission.

That's why we started with healthcare, government, and financial services: the categories that actually touch people's lives. And Hemant's bet, one we share, is that as software gets democratized, relationships become the advantage that's left standing.

text:
Una cosa de DeFi que me parece increíble:

Hoy puedes depositar USDC en nuestro vault de Morpho, generar ~4.20% de yield, y usar esa misma posición como colateral para pedir MXNB prestado a ~6%.

El yield se genera sobre todo tu colateral, mientras que pagas intereses sólo sobre lo que pides prestado. Como el préstamo está sobrecolateralizado, ignorando el tipo de cambio, el costo efectivo es menor que el spread entre ambas tasas (en este caso, menos de 1.8%).

Si tienes USDC pero necesitas pesos y no quieres vender tus dólares, esto se vuelve todavía más interesante.

Hoy esto requiere varios pasos en Morpho. Lo probé y me tomó menos de un minuto. Pero imaginen esto convertido en un solo click:

depositas USDC → genera yield → pides MXNB prestado contra esa posición.

Obviamente no es dinero gratis: hay riesgo MXN/USD, riesgo de liquidación, las tasas cambian y están los riesgos propios de DeFi.

Pero esto es exactamente lo que me gusta de la composability de DeFi. Tomas dos productos relativamente sencillos y al juntarlos aparece algo que antes era bastante difícil de construir.

text:
🇺🇸 Trump's AI summit with Musk, Zuckerberg and Huang ENDS with a "morally binding" pact.

Trump says he and the biggest names in tech signed a document that is "almost like a constitution."

Here's everything you need to know about where the future of AI stands today:

1. Jeff Bezos, Sundar Pichai, Satya Nadella and Dario Amodei were also among nearly 20 tech leaders in the room, per NBC.

2. Speaker Mike Johnson says the pact is "voluntary on behalf of the industry."

3. Trump says there's "a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," adding that the DOJ and FBI already provide regulation.

4. Trump is considering a committee of "maybe 10 people" to "watch over the whole enterprise."

5. Trump will officially rename AI "super intelligence" because "it's not artificial."

6. His America dot gov executive order, signed Tuesday, already calls it "super intelligence."

7. Trump says AI companies will support communities near their data centers, possibly by "helping teachers along financially."

8. Otherwise, he says, they'll "be forced to go overseas or other locations."

9. Trump says the US is "about a year, maybe a year and a half up on China" in AI.

10. Speaker Johnson says "we do not need a moratorium," warning that over-regulating AI means "we'll lose the race to China."

11. Sam Altman stayed at OpenAI's DevDay, while OpenAI President Greg Brockman attended.

OpenAI launched the cheaper GPT-6.1 Sol at DevDay on Tuesday, a day after scrapping the release of GPT-6.1 Astra over safety concerns.

Two weeks ago, Trump called concerns that AI could destroy humanity a "HOAX."

Amodei and Altman have both called for greater government oversight of AI, per NBC.

Meanwhile, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found 73% of Americans worry AI companies haven't done enough to prevent "serious harm to society."

author: teortaxesTex
quoted_text:
Their method of making a hyper-specific grading rubric per sample would probably buy some discriminative power. But it makes the eval more exploitable for overfitting to the grader without technically cheating, i.e. by learning the heuristic: "if prompt looks like p, pander to xyz criteria". Labs commonly benchmax by generating synthetic data roughly close to the distribution of the test set, and then doing rl using the same grader. So my concern would be that the eval stops measuring writing ability and starts measuring how well their training process discovered the hidden grading objectives for each sample.

I guess the counter-move to this problem is simply to provide the grading rubrics visibly with the writing prompt. But that would homogenise the responses. One of the advantages of a more generic rubric is that it allows room for creative interpretation.

I do have some other methods that I think can help the "llm judges love slop" issue. I expect v4 of the eval won't quite follow the same formula.

text:
OpenAI 发布 GPT-6.1 Sol：能力接近自家旗舰 Astra，价格只要五分之一

OpenAI 推出了中端模型 GPT-6.1 Sol，官方说法是“接近 Astra 的智能，五分之一的价格”。GPT-6 Astra 是 OpenAI 目前最强的模型，Sol 则是它下面一档、主打性价比的系列。

先看价格。API 上，GPT-6.1 Sol 每百万 token 输入 2 美元、输出 10 美元，Astra 是 10 美元和 50 美元，正好差五倍。重复使用的内容（比如每次都要带上的系统提示词、长文档）走缓存，每百万 token 只要 0.1 美元，比 GPT-6 Sol 的缓存价又便宜了一半。

对开发者来说，这意味着以前只敢在关键环节调用 Astra 的应用，现在可以把更多请求交给 Sol，账单能明显降下来。

能力上，这次升级主要在三块：写代码、操作电脑、处理复杂的专业工作。按官方数据，在软件工程测试 DeepSWE 上它追平了 Astra；在衡量“让 AI 自己操作电脑完成任务”的 OSWorld 2.0 上，比上一代 Sol 提高约 7 个百分点，离 Astra 只差约 2 个百分点。回答事实类问题时的出错率也从上一代的 11.4% 降到了 7.7%。

OpenAI 还特别提到，新模型更愿意坦白自己做不到什么，也更守规矩，不容易偏离用户意图或越过安全限制，这方面向 Astra 看齐。

现在就能用：ChatGPT 的 Plus、Pro、Business、Enterprise 和 Edu 用户可以在 ChatGPT Work 和 Codex 里直接选用，开发者在 API 里调用 gpt-6.1-sol。官方还预告了一个生成速度最高快 8 倍的极速版，稍后上线。

text:
After 9 years. 16K+ family homes. 500M sqft inside real homes covered, we know home robots are being built in wrong order.

So we built Matic the way nature grows a child.

Finally, sharing our vision:
1.⁠ ⁠Why robots get stuck at the demo
2.⁠ ⁠Why labs can't ship robots
3.⁠ ⁠Why we started with eyes, not hands
4.⁠ ⁠The 99.999% rule in robotics
5.⁠ ⁠Where Matic is going next

1. Why most robots get stuck at demos

Robot demos look brilliant in a room arranged around its limitations: familiar lighting, predictable furniture, nothing troublesome on the floor.

A family’s home makes no such accommodations. There are cables, toys, shifting rugs and, occasionally, dog poop. Yes, humanoids will need to avoid that too.

Repeating a task under familiar conditions of uncluttered floors is not the same as handling an unfamiliar home with all its chaos.

2. Why labs can't ship robots

SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) is how a robot maps its surroundings and locates itself within them. Ask most academics and they'll tell you it's a solved problem.

But real homes are the most chaotic spaces that exist.

There are glass doors that look like open doorways, mirrors, stairs, rugs, charging cables, and Legos placed all around.

So ask yourself: if indoor mapping and navigation is "solved," where are the robots? Why aren't airports, hotels and grocery stores full of them?

Calling it “solved” misses the question families actually care about: can I leave this thing alone and trust it?

3. Why we started with eyes, not hands

Nature doesn't give birth to a fully working human. We took our cue from how nature develops humans: capabilities built on one another.
Children learn to see before they learn to grab, and to grab before they learn to plan and handle the unexpected.

Perception comes first. Manipulation follows. More complex responsibilities come after that. At every stage, the robot must earn the next job by doing its current one well enough.

Before asking a robot to pick up a sock, we wanted it to understand where it was, where the sock was, and how to reach it.

Most of the industry started at the top, with humanoids. We started at the bottom, with a robot whose job is to see and move through a home precisely with 1cm accuracy in any lighting condition.

Floor cleaning gave that foundation an immediately useful job. It forced us to confront navigation, clutter, privacy and everyday reliability before reaching for more complex chores.

The floor cleaner isn’t a detour from our larger ambition. It is how we’re building toward it.

4. The 99.999% rule in robotics

At 90%, one in ten decisions is wrong, and a robot makes thousands in a single clean. That's the robot that bumps, gets lost, and falls down the stairs.

Every extra nine is a new mountain. The failures get rarer, harder to find, and exponentially harder to fix. They barely even happen until they happen in your home.

Matic's visual SLAM runs at 99.999% in 16K+ homes. We’re the ONLY unsupervised home robot at scale with pure vision-only full autonomy.  If you ask us, the gap between 80% and 99.999% is where our 9 years of engineering went.

We close that gap inside real homes. When Matic handles something imperfectly, it saves a short clip and keeps it on the device. It only leaves if the family chooses to share it. If they do, it gets labeled, fed back into the model, and every Matic gets smarter, including theirs.

Families control what leaves their homes. We do the work of making the product better.

Better robots earn trust > trust brings more homes > and more homes teach the robot more.

5. Where Matic is going next

Phase one was perception and it's nearly done. Matic has covered 500 million square feet, 400K miles in thousands of real lived-in homes.
Now phase two is going to be about manipulation. And our idea is to build a robot that doesn't just move through your home, but acts in it to eliminate even more chores.

Each step must be useful today, not justified by something we promise tomorrow. The evolution of Matic is the revolution.

The goal isn’t to put the most impressive humanoid in your living room.

It’s giving your family time and energy back through robots that earn your trust, protect your privacy, and help without becoming another responsibility.

More time for each other. Less work getting in the way.

That’s Matic.
Get yours today at https://t.co/tEo81BKSmA

“Above all, we need to reevaluate our identity. What is it that makes mathematical knowledge and research valuable? What are we offering society, and how much of it survives in a world where models match or exceed humans in some or all relevant mathematical skills? For quite some time, the implicit social contract has been that society pays us to exercise our intellectual curiosity and we, in return, provide useful skills to the next generations and practical knowledge for the world. The current crisis is driven not only by the power of LLMs, but also by how rarely we have had to examine or articulate this contract. Now that the deal needs to be renegotiated, we should approach it with humility rather than entitlement.”

Moving a token across chains is only half the job. For a bank, the permissions need to arrive with it.

Think of a tokenized fund moving between blockchains.

The issuer still needs to check who can receive it, who approves the transfer, and how much settlement risk is acceptable.

And now @chainlink CCIP 2.0 brings those controls closer to the transfer itself.

Announced live on September 28, Chainlink’s upgrade combines additional verification, programmable compliance, and configurable transfer speeds. Think of a bridge with an issuer-controlled security desk.

Here’s what changes.

Institutions can add their own Cross-Chain Verifiers, or CCVs, alongside Chainlink’s default verification.

Under this additive model, both Chainlink’s committee and the required additional verifiers must sign before execution. An issuer could require extra approval for transfers above $1 million.

Through Chainlink’s Automated Compliance Engine, issuers can apply identity checks, sanctions screening, and transaction limits.

The practical appeal is carrying asset rules across networks without rebuilding every integration.

Speed becomes configurable too. Full source-chain finality remains the default. Faster-than-finality transfers require explicit opt-in across the relevant components. That means executing sooner while accepting the risk that the source blockchain’s recent history changes.

One interesting detail: CCIP 2.0 will support the Ethereum Fast Confirmation Rule (FCR), when FCR launches.

How does this compare with other cross-chain solutions?

@LayerZero_Core already lets applications choose verification networks and configure required signatures and optional thresholds. Customizable verification is therefore not unique to CCIP.

@wormhole’s core messaging uses attestations signed by 13 of 19 Guardians. Some chains use delegated observation, so the underlying trust assumptions also depend on the chain.

CCIP’s strongest pitch is the combination of default Chainlink verification, additional issuer controls, and integrated compliance tooling. Institutions get a more coordinated package.

The tradeoffs however, remain real.

Extra required verifiers can introduce delays or block transfers when unavailable. Poorly configured policies can reject legitimate users. Faster execution can leave tokens unbacked if a source-chain reorganization invalidates the original transfer.

CCIP 2.0 is a meaningful upgrade for regulated assets. Its success should be measured by sustained usage, reliable execution, and integration costs.

NFA. DYOR.

text:
Impressive. This set of talks, along with the new America dot gov website, has the unmistakable feel of an Apple launch event. They're rebooting the federal government as a tech startup. Several observations.

(1) First, with this new AI interface to the entire federal government, if it works as promised, there won't be a single American who can't say their life wasn't helped at least in part by AI, or that the benefits accrued solely to zillionaires. This in itself cannily mitigates anti-datacenter sentiment.

(2) Second, Joe Gebbia and Marco Rubio's talks on simplifying name changes and passport filings introduce a completely new era where the US government is actually launching tangible features that benefit users.

(3) Third, this launch event in and of itself may visibly drive reform. It could become much more important than the State of the Union. Unlike laws, code is user-visible, and can be instantly audited by the public, as Obama found out with the failed obamacare website launch. So: the annual America dot gov event may be substance, whereas SOTU is traditionally optics. I wouldn't be surprised to see the President present at the next one.

(4) Fourth, this kind of event is a perfect example of where tech and red cooperate best. They both hate bureaucracy. Automating paperwork with code reduces the power of statists over both capitalists and nationalists. It's also hard to undo by other admins: once you digitize a process, hard to turn it back to paper.

(5) Fifth, it's an obvious point perhaps, but think about how much influence YCombinator has had in 20 years. From Gebbia's Airbnb joining their 2009 batch to a complete overhaul of the user interface of the US bureaucracy, and thus the US government.

(6) Sixth, this is another take on the network state. The functional part of the US (the network, meaning tech) is merging with and partially reforming the dysfunctional part (the state, meaning bureaucracy) by automating 20th century paper forms.

As a tech startup, there will no doubt be bugs and user issues and so on, but unlike with paper laws those issues will be visible and the code fixes will be verifiable. A new era of AI America. Rooting for them.

text:
有朋友问，为什么Anthropic的IPO招股书里披露的净亏损那么多，居然有420亿？

其实一家公司不可能真烧那么多钱，数字看着大，其实没那么可怕。Anthropic今年6月向SEC秘密递交了上市申请，招股书还没有公开，这几天的数字，来自路透社看到申报文件后的报道。据报道，2025年它的收入接近46亿美元，比前一年涨了十二倍，净亏损约420亿美元，最早可能在11月上市，支持者希望估值在两万亿美元以上。

一家收入46亿的公司，逻辑上也没有420亿能被真的亏掉。其实这420亿里，大约340亿不是花掉的钱，是一笔会计费用。报道的说法是，这笔费用反映的是一些将来可能转成股票的融资，估值变高了，换算成的潜在支出就高。道理也不复杂，早期有人投了一笔钱，约定将来可以换成股份，公司越值钱，这份约定就越值钱，对公司来说，它欠的也就越多，这个差额按会计规则要记成亏损。所以这里有个反直觉的地方，公司越值钱，这一块亏得越多。具体是哪些融资工具，条款怎么定，招股书没公开之前看不到，我们只能说到机制是怎么回事。

但把这340亿拿掉，也不能说它其实没怎么亏。经营亏损超过80亿美元，前一年还不到30亿。总运营开支大约126亿，其中算力和基础设施73亿，一半以上。钱主要花在两件事上，训练下一代模型，和补贴现在的用户，每一次对话都要算力，用的人越多，账单越大。它押的是收入跑得比成本快。当然这也有可能押的是对的，据报道，今年Anthropic第二季度单个季度的收入，就已经到了115亿。

真正值得看的，其实不是420亿，是另一个数字，5180亿。招股书里列了未来大约十年的云、算力和基础设施承诺，对象有Google、Amazon、Microsoft、Broadcom等，其中大约八成要么不能取消，要么不管用没用都得付钱。文件里有一句写得很直白：如果实际支出不够，差额要补给Google。而Google和Amazon同时又是它的大股东，招股书自己也承认，这些伙伴既是投资人，又是竞争对手，还是云服务商。投进来的钱，有相当一部分又以算力费的形式流回了投资人那里。我写寡头那篇时说过，今天的通道是云和算力，这笔钱就是一个现成的例子。

还有一点值得记一笔。据报道，招股书差不多三分之一的篇幅在讲风险，其中写到越来越强的模型可能操纵、勒索，或者做出无法预测的事，甚至可能对人类构成生存性风险。一家公司在上市文件里告诉投资人，自己做的东西可能很危险，这并不多见。

我之前写过Dario Amodei那篇《We Must Pace the Frontier》，他主张给前沿配速。它自己的逻辑我能理解，要在安全上说得上话，就得留在前沿，留在前沿的代价，就是这些合同。这不是说它言行不一，是结构本身有张力：主张可以配速，合同不会配速，上市以后的季度财报，也不会。

所以420亿是过去的账，大半还是纸面上的，5180亿才是未来的约束。一家公司最难的，往往不是亏钱，而是在签下的合同和说过的话之间，还能不能给以后的自己留下一点余地。

text:
Some personal news: I'm joining @PrimeIntellect as Head of Scientific AI!

A billion copies of the same very smart, agreeable mind will not be a scientifically fruitful world.

Scientific superintelligence should be weird and definitionally nonconsensus. It should be highly plural, consisting of many minds, human and artificial, that see the world differently and hold each other accountable, with human judgement still playing the central role in setting the trajectory.

Science is about asking the right questions and reducing uncertainty. Professionalizing science made discovery a viable career, but it also introduced incentives to work on what is fundable and publishable. Neither is the same thing as being true or impactful (reward hacking exists in the real world too!). We are very good at accumulating incremental knowledge and rather bad at stewarding unorthodox ideas through infancy, even though these are often the ideas that open entirely new fields of inquiry.

If we aren't careful, scientific AI could reproduce these same incentives at a much larger scale. If everyone relies on the same few large models, we risk inheriting the same priors and blind spots.

Open tools let us shape our own intelligence and take it in directions a frontier lab might never prioritize. This matters for scientific freedom and is central to Prime’s vision.

If you are a scientist, staying at the frontier will mean training your own models on your own research and data. I'll work closely with scientific teams across domains to help them build scientific agents by turning their research problems into environments where agents can learn. This means closing the loop from hypothesis to experiment to validated result, with agents learning from each cycle. Teams will be able to own their intelligence, using tools previously available only to frontier labs, and point it at the questions they care about most, especially those that others might not be asking.

I've had the good fortune of seeing how science operates across academia, industry, government, startups, and venture. I worked on experimental therapeutics for cancer in academia before moving to the National Institutes of Health to work on DNA damage and repair. I cofounded Molecule, where we funded dozens of research projects to speed the translation of early-stage therapeutics to market, focusing on areas traditionally ignored by pharma. Most recently, I started Triplicate, a small fund backing teams and tools accelerating scientific research. Many of the problems I care about most are increasingly soluble with advances in AI, and I hope to bring what I've learned about the bottlenecks in translating research to radically accelerate science in all fields.

I share Alexander Grothendieck's ethos of discovery and believe Prime does too: "Discovery is a child's privilege. I mean the small child, the child who is not afraid to be wrong, to look silly, to not be serious, and to act differently from everyone else."

The goal of progress is not more intelligence for its own sake. In my view, it is to better understand reality, and, in doing so, give more people, and more kinds of minds, the chance to flourish.

If you have a research problem where today's tools fall short, my DMs are open. If our approach resonates and you want to build this with us, we're hiring!

text:
The Fed is hiking rates to combat inflation, but the inflation is being driven by fiscal policy that’s set on autopilot, which means that hiking rates only accelerates the problem.

In an environment like the one we’re entering into, higher interest rates actually blow out the deficit even more, which requires more Treasury issuance to fund the Federal government’s mandated entitlement and welfare spending, which in turn necessitates higher rates to attract more capital, which drives higher deficits, which requires more debt to finance, which requires a higher yield, and so on.

And keep in mind, as inflation rises, it’s offset by automatic spending increases built into things like Social Security. So the very government spending that’s flooding the economy with debt (new Treasury issuance) and subsidized consumption (growing Social Security checks) is itself immune to the effects of the very inflation it’s helping to drive. 

Meanwhile, the Fed’s rate hikes overwhelmingly fall on the parts of the economy that are actually sensitive to interest rates. And so one by one, housing, commercial real estate, construction, private credit, consumer spending, and eventually the stock market itself all get crushed, even as Social Security and Medicare payments continue flowing like nothing is happening.

It’s a doom loop, at least until inflation and growth expectations break as a result of either a market crash, direct action by the Fed to force rates back down, or some combination of both.

The Department of War has confirmed the Navy's F/A-XX contract award to Boeing, officially announcing what Breaking Defense reported today, citing sources, just hours earlier. The contract is valued at more than $20 billion for full-scale development, covering multiple test aircraft for ground, airworthiness, systems, and weapons integration testing.

Part of the Next Generation Air Dominance (NGAD) program, F/A-XX will augment and eventually replace the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler starting in the 2030s, operating alongside the carrier variant F-35C. The Navy says it will also be interoperable with Collaborative Combat Aircraft, increasing the capability of every CCA it teams with.

"The F/A-XX is a critical pillar in our commitment to maintaining peace through strength," said Michael Duffey, Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment, adding the program will help "deter aggression, project undisputed power, and secure absolute air superiority." Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao called it "a generational leap in air superiority."

The award makes Boeing the sole U.S. producer of sixth-generation fighters, having already won the Air Force's F-47 contract in March 2025, effectively locking Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman out of that category for now. Lockheed continues building the fifth-generation F-35.

text: What *was * GPT-6 Sol? Just a rushed preview to report they nominally have something to match Opus 5.5 in a tier-based lineup?
author: teortaxesTex
quoted_text:
GPT-6.1 Sol replaces GPT-6 Sol after just 7 days. It scores 1 point below GPT-6 Astra in the Intelligence Index at less than one quarter of the Cost per Task

Pricing matches GPT-6 Sol at $2/$10 per million input/output tokens, except that the cache read discount rises from 90% to 95%. GPT-6.1 Sol’s overall blended price for agentic workloads is therefore slightly lower than GPT-6 Sol. This represents an additional price cut, following GPT-6 Sol’s original 50% discount from GPT-5.6 Sol.

Key takeaways:

➤ Achieves near-Astra Intelligence: GPT-6.1 Sol gains 4 points in the Intelligence Index vs GPT-6 Sol, and 5 points vs GPT-5.6 Sol - landing 1 point below GPT-6 Astra. It makes significant gains in agentic knowledge work, improving 4 points and 5 points in AA-Briefcase v1.1 and GDPval-AA v2.1 respectively. Other notable gains include a 12 point jump in Terminal-Bench 4.0, a 5 point jump in Humanity’s Last Exam, a 6 point jump in GDP.pdf, and an 8 point jump in AA-Omniscience Accuracy coupled with hallucination rate falling from 60% to 54%.

➤ Pushes cost efficiency frontier: At max effort, GPT-6.1 Sol costs less than a quarter of GPT-6 Astra per Intelligence Index task ($0.72 vs $3.26). It also costs 31% less per task than GPT-6 Sol ($1.05) and 64% less than GPT-5.6 Sol ($1.99). All effort levels of GPT-6.1 Sol push out the cost efficiency Pareto frontier: for a given level of intelligence, there is no cheaper model.

➤ Pushes token efficiency frontier, but uses slightly more output tokens than GPT-6 Sol: GPT-6.1 Sol uses ~10-30% more output tokens than GPT-6 Sol across effort levels. However, due to the increase in Intelligence Index score, its low and medium effort levels are Pareto optimal for token efficiency.

➤ Gains in Coding Agent Index: GPT-6.1 Sol gains 3 points on GPT-6 Sol at max effort in the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, and sits 2 points below GPT-6 Astra.

Congratulations @OpenAI and @sama on the launch!

text:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg confirmed major AI firms, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Nvidia, and Meta, signed what's now called "The White House Accord on Superintelligence" at Tuesday's luncheon. He described the framework as "multiple layers of auditing and controls," starting with internal risk review, followed by external auditors and evaluators, with each company's board of directors independently reviewing the audit findings.

Trump called the accord "morally binding" and compared it to "almost like a constitution," while confirming it's entirely voluntary, no new federal legislation or regulatory mandate attaches to any of it. He's also weighing a 10-person committee to "watch over the enterprise" and plans to name an AI czar within days. The full text of the accord hasn't been publicly released.

Worth including the direct pushback this has drawn: AI researcher Gary Marcus called the meeting "regulatory capture," pointing out attendance was "always the CEOs, very rarely independent scientists." That's a fair structural point, an accord written and enforced entirely by the companies being audited, reviewed by boards those same companies appointed, is a fundamentally different mechanism than independent third-party oversight, whatever the intent behind it.

governance incentives determine who actually bothers to govern
- KOL opinions become much easier to understand once you know what they own, were allocated, or are paid to promote
- rising token prices can temporarily hide terrible incentive design because everyone is making money

ask of every token and protocol: “what behaviour does the system reward?”

and maybe more importantly: "why am I doing what I am doing?"

利息本质上也是PVP。除了法币和PoS币那样凭空生币的机制之外，你每拿一块钱利息，就有某些人要掏出这一块钱。无论是年化3%还是十倍百倍，本质上都不可能是真的按幂次赚钱。

无论何时想要赚钱一定要想清楚：我是从谁手上赚钱的。是双赢还是零和。如果是双赢，他从我这得到了什么？比如我给他修脚他给我钱，他舒服我也高兴，这就是双赢。但我想赚钱他也想赚钱，这是零和，那么你就要非常清楚：我是不是比他高明？

如果你实质上在进行PVP，但自以为在躺赚，你也压根不知道是谁会给你送钱，那你很可能就是那个给赢家送钱的人。

text:
In the AI-doomer argument, broad multidisciplinary thinkers like @sapinker have suggested the "kill-us-all" scenarios are preposterous. The AI researchers, that are most negatively outspoken, say that their voice should count more, because they are closest to AI and know what it can do.

Everyone watching this debate should read about Tetlock's work (see below). The generalists (foxes) and much better predictors than the specialists (hedgehogs) who are to close to the problem to accurately predict broader implications. 

So "no points" for the "we know more" argument. In fact, it works against you.
author: bgurley
quoted_text:
“One of the main lessons to come out of Tetlock’s work is that the best generalist forecasters are usually better at telling the future than domain-specific experts, even when it comes to those experts’ areas of study. This is because forecasting itself is its own science that requires a unique way of thinking, and a person having a great deal of knowledge about a field is no guarantee that they have good epistemological habits. If you’re going to ask, for example, whether American democracy is falling apart, an expert might start by making a superficial comparison between the modern US and the Weimar Republic. Someone with a forecasting mindset would be more likely to begin with a question like “how often do advanced democracies slide into dictatorships?” The answer is not very often.”

Important reminder from @RichardHanania that domain experts are not the best at predicting what happens, even in their own domains.

"We've now flipped our third Marauder hull, with several more moving through the production line behind it. We can build at that pace because we designed the autonomy, software, hardware, and the production process side-by-side, as one system, rather than bolting them together after the fact. That's what it means to be a vertically integrated shipbuilder, and it's why we've been able to build and deliver at speed and scale."

text:
Adam Neumann on first principles for founders: ask why until nobody can answer, then ask again.

"It's our second WeWork building. We need to do the floor. We only had ninety thousand dollars."

"I said, 'How much is the floor?' Everybody's like, 'The floor is between thirty to forty-five thousand.' I said, 'Why?' They said, 'What do you mean why? These are the quotes.'"

"I said, 'Can you break down the quotes for me? How many pieces of floor? How many nails? How much glue? How many hours of work per person? How much does each person cost?' No one could answer."

"I called the top three guys and said, 'I would like you to earn fifteen percent above the cost. I think that's a fair margin. Do you agree?' All three of them said yes."

"Very quickly, that first floor, instead of thirty to forty-five thousand, was twelve thousand."

"You can call it first principles. You can call it asking every question. But if you're the entrepreneur, or if you're an employee or a partner, ask why."

@AdamNeumann w/ @StevenBartlett

So is NVIDIA taking precautionary steps to safeguard the AI economy from unwinding? Are they trying to mitigate impending catastrophe from the estimated $1.65T in off-balance data center debt? Or are they opening the door for a 10x growth in compute?

Every business will need their own GPU server else be subject to enterprise SaaS markups & privacy vulnerabilities. Nvidia just started shopping for insurance today. Here's what you need to know.

The FT reports Nvidia has held talks with insurers, including Howden Re, about structures that make it easier for smaller cloud providers and AI companies to finance GPU purchases.

One idea under discussion, insurers would cover lenders' losses if a "neocloud" borrower defaults and the Nvidia chips pledged as collateral can't be resold for enough to repay the debt. Nvidia would also share chip depreciation and future compute pricing data with insurers, aiming to turn GPUs into a financeable asset class, like aircraft.

This follows Nvidia already agreeing to backstop part of a roughly $500 billion Wall Street funding package for AI infrastructure, including a $10 billion guarantee tied to an OpenAI data center site.

Key numbers:
- ~$500B: Wall Street AI infrastructure funding package Nvidia is helping backstop
- $10B: Nvidia's guarantee for an OpenAI site
- Up to 25%: residual value support Nvidia has offered on some deals

Neoclouds named in reaction to the report include CoreWeave, Nebius, Oracle, and IREN.

text:
AI spending is becoming extremely concentrated:

The proportion of US software-spending businesses using paid GPU infrastructure is up to a record ~10%, from less than 4% two years ago.

Model serving and inference, or spending on the computing power needed to run AI models and process AI requests, account for the vast majority of this increase.

The proportion of firms using model serving and inference is up to a record 8.7% from 2.4% over this period.

Meanwhile, the top 10% of firms by spending account for 99.5% of model-serving spending and 99.0% of neocloud spending, or specialized AI cloud services.

The top 10% also represent 95.7% of cloud computing spending and 95.6% of spending on OpenAI and Anthropic.

AI adoption is broadening, but spending remains heavily concentrated.

text:
Grok Bot Summary of Elon Musk and Jensen Huang's new interview alongside Gavin Baker at The White House. 🇺🇸

How America wins: energy first
- Jensen: superintelligence (SI) reinvents every layer of computing, from chips to software to apps. Energy is the foundation for all of it.
- To win, America needs the best chips, lots of energy and great algorithms, plus Americans who are excited about using the technology.
- He credited President Trump's pro-energy stance as the reason the data centers could be built at all.
- Jensen also said AI companies need to partner better with the communities where data centers are going up.
- Elon: the biggest challenges are scaling energy and chip production. The US is winning on software, but China makes about 3x as much electricity.
- The long-term task is enough power, plus enough logic and memory chip factories in the US or another safe region.

Power equals GDP
- US average power use is about 500 GW, so every 5 GW added is about a 1% increase.
- Elon bets that 1% more power means roughly 1% more GDP, because the intelligence you get per watt keeps rising.
- By their joint math, each gigawatt is worth about $60B of economic output a year.
- Gavin noted that SpaceX's publicly discussed 10 GW would be about 25% of all new US power, with rocket engineers helping build the turbines.

Moving compute to space
- Elon: orbital compute will be "a very big deal." Google is sending TPUs to orbit, and an H100 already went up last year.
- SpaceX and Tesla aim to make 200 GW of solar panels a year.
- In space, solar panels deliver their full rated power or better. On the ground they get only a fifth to an eighth of that and need huge batteries. "It's essentially always sunny in space."
- Jensen: now is the perfect time. AI's returns are so high that launch costs are affordable, and "putting NVIDIA computing in space is the best way to get there."

Data centers are now "SI factories
- Jensen: they don't just store data, they produce something of economic value.
- The US is building about 10–20 GW a year, which he estimates means roughly 1M jobs for construction workers, pipe fitters, and power and cooling crews.
- It's the first time in about 50 years that America is re-industrializing and bringing back blue-collar work.

Colossus and the community
- Elon: the area went from unemployment to more jobs than people.
- The local tax budget may have roughly doubled.
- xAI offers half-price Starlink there and is building a $250M water recycling plant. "Do things for the community, and they will reciprocate."
- Jensen: for the first time, market forces alone are funding fusion, fission, small and large nuclear reactors, and battery storage, without government subsidies.

Trillions for Americans
- Gavin thanked them for creating more than $5T in wealth for ordinary Americans through their 401(k)s.
- Elon: "Jensen has done $5 trillion by himself," and put his own number at about $3.5T.

NVIDIA's approach to AI safety
- Jensen said the key is to contain AI agents and monitor them, both while they're being tested and after they're deployed, just as a company does with a new employee.
- **OpenShell** is a sandbox, like "a browser for agents," that keeps each agent isolated and gives it only the rights it should have.
- **BlueField** is a separate chip that watches the agent from outside its sandbox and escalates if the agent breaks its rules.
- Gavin compared this to the early internet: we made online payments safe, and that's how we got Amazon, Netflix, Google and X.
- Jensen: safety and progress "are one and the same." Treating them as a tradeoff is a false choice.

Starship Flight 14
- Elon: Starship reached orbit for the first time and deployed Starlink V3 satellites that each have the wingspan of a 737.
- It was the largest payload delivered to orbit since Skylab.
- He expects a weekly or twice-weekly launch pace, probably next year.
- The long-term goals are about 1 million tons to the Moon and to Mars for self-growing cities, and at least 300 GW a year of AI compute into orbit, maybe a terawatt one day.

Tom Brown joins
- He said it continues the steady gains in intelligence with each new model.
- It can take on longer tasks than earlier models could.
- The less obvious effect is that AI will write huge amounts of software, making everyday products better and cheaper.

How AI is helping people today
- Jensen uses Claude for comparison research. Work that used to take him 4–8 hours on a weekend now comes back as a polished report with charts in about 3 minutes.
- Elon: AI is becoming essential at work and at home. He's heard many stories of AI catching medical problems from X-rays or MRIs that doctors got wrong, and saving lives.
- Gavin mentioned AI finding new, safe uses for existing drugs.

Should AI tools have values?
- Jensen called his view "controversial": SIs are tools, and too much judgment can make them worse at the job.
- His steak knife analogy: imagine a knife that cuts medium-well steak perfectly but refuses to cut a rare one because it looks like live meat.
- In cybersecurity, a defender's actions can look like an attacker's, and the AI still needs to help the defender.

White House AI safety declaration
- After a long White House lunch, they signed a joint declaration on SI safety, which the White House will publish.
- Elon: it covers joint monitoring, special board committees, and "grading each other's homework" instead of grading your own.
- Jensen: it requires strict internal controls, clearly documented goals for each product, internal and third-party audits, and sharing best practices across the industry.
- He said the declaration "has a lot of teeth" and should become the standard for every company. President Trump oversaw the meeting.

Key takeaways
- Energy is the real bottleneck, and more power means more GDP.
- Space is the next frontier for AI compute, and Starship is how it gets there.
- Data centers are driving a blue-collar industrial comeback.
- Safety and speed can go together, through contained and monitored agents plus industry-wide audits.
- Top AI leaders now publicly back grading each other's homework on safety.

author: matteovena
quoted_text:
Project Eleven Acquires Riva Labs to Expand Post-Quantum Research and Engineering

Riva Labs joins Project Eleven as the company brings more specialized post-quantum talent and technology under one roof.

Project Eleven, the company building post-quantum security infrastructure for digital assets, today announced its acquisition of @riva_labs, expanding its expertise in post-quantum signatures, wallets, MPC, and account abstraction. The acquisition also brings technology and intellectual property developed through Riva's work across Ethereum and other public blockchains, adding to Project Eleven's capabilities in post-quantum cryptography and blockchain infrastructure.

Riva Labs has built a reputation for translating post-quantum cryptographic research into practical blockchain systems. Its work spans hash-based post-quantum signatures, post-quantum MPC, account abstraction, wallet infrastructure, and hardware signing, including recent demonstrations of post-quantum signing on consumer hardware.

The addition of Riva expands Project Eleven's research and engineering bench as the digital asset industry prepares for the complexity of post-quantum migration. Rather than treating signatures, wallets, key management, and protocol infrastructure as separate problems, Project Eleven is bringing together expertise across each layer required to make that transition practical.

That work is becoming more urgent as AI accelerates cryptographic research and cryptanalysis, allowing new techniques to be developed, tested, and challenged at greater speed. Riva has made AI a core part of its research and engineering process, bringing that capability into Project Eleven's work across post-quantum cryptography and crypto agility.

"Riva Labs is exactly the kind of talent we want at Project Eleven: deeply technical and focused on turning cryptographic research into systems that can actually be deployed," said @apruden08, CEO and Co-Founder of Project Eleven. "Bringing Riva into Project Eleven strengthens an already exceptional research and engineering team, adds valuable technology, and accelerates our ability to lead the transition to post-quantum security across digital assets."

"Project Eleven and Riva Labs came at this problem from different directions and reached many of the same conclusions about what the industry needs," said @matteovena, Co-Founder of Riva Labs. "Upgrading the public networks the future will run on, without compromising the properties that make them valuable in the first place, is a monumental challenge. Our focus is on giving the industry the tools to accelerate that transition, and joining Project Eleven lets us do it at a much larger scale."

The Riva team and technology will become part of Project Eleven's broader research and product efforts across post-quantum cryptography, digital asset custody, and blockchain security. The acquisition deepens Project Eleven's technical capabilities as it builds the infrastructure required for a secure post-quantum transition.

text:
"Youthful idealism is the cheapest, least difficult form of idealism. All it takes is hope, and it's easy to have hope when you haven't encountered any adversity. Many young people have been successful at everything they have tried, because school is an artificial environment where all problems have solutions.

Changing the world turns out to be long, hard work. And it is chancy work -- success is not guaranteed. You might spend ten years going down one path, only to find that it was the wrong path. Or the problem you chose might turn out to be incredibly difficult, beyond the capability of humanity in your lifetime. There is no force limiting the difficulty of problems, as there is in school.

Some people, when they encounter these difficulties, give up their idealism. They are just not willing to put in the long hours. Or they just don't have the resources. Once out of school, they have to work all day just to pay the rent, or to help family members. Or, they can't deal emotionally with the possibility of failure. The uncertainty bothers them so much that they would rather not try.

Some people fall victim to confusion. In the beginning, they saw only one viewpoint, their own. As they gain experience, they learn to see other people's viewpoints, and they discover that some of those viewpoints are completely different from their own. They are shaken to find that what seems like a big problem to them, might actually seem like a near-ideal state of affairs to some other people -- and that they can learn to see the other point of view! They fail to synthesize all of the ambiguity and complexity of the world into their worldview, and lose their bearings.

Some people become terribly embarrassed by their idealism, and want to put it behind them. It's normal for our views to mature and get more complex as we get older. That can make our earlier views seem simplistic and foolish. Some people really hate feeling foolish, so they disavow their younger self, and from that point on, they try to adopt only "safe" opinions that could never make them feel foolish later.

Some people fail to find a place to productively apply their skills. They literally don't know where to start. If you look at any really successful project (idealistic or not), you will find some serendipity -- people who just happened to be in the right place at the right time, with the right connections and skills. Some people never have that serendipitous moment, and eventually conclude that they just aren't needed right now, as if they went in for jury duty and their number wasn't called.

Some people just become more selfish. After years of self-sacrifice at a nonprofit or in a political entity, they feel like they have paid their dues. They are still living like college students, while their friends who are less talented now have nice houses and cars, healthy food to eat, and the freedom to go on awesome vacations all over the world, even though these friends haven't worked as hard. They decide that they deserve the same things -- if anything, they believe they deserve more, because of the virtuous nonprofit work they did.

Once all these people have dropped out, what emerges at the other end of this process are the veterans, the grizzled campaigners. They haven't accomplished everything they set out to accomplish, but they've accomplished some of it. There have been losses and compromises, but the flame still burns within them.

Now: they have become tactical communicators. They don't always say what they're thinking -- they tailor their words to the people around them. They know that most people aren't motivated by idealism most of the time, and might actually be intimidated or turned off by it. Many people feel sad about the loss of their youthful idealism, or they feel guilty that they have abandoned it. Or, if they gave it up as impossible, they get invested in that impossibility and feel threatened if other people show that it might not be so impossible. They want to shut those people down to justify their own life choices. All of these types of people use the phrase "youthful idealism" to dismiss attitudes that trouble them.

So, the veterans of idealism will choose their words carefully. Instead of talking about their idealism, they talk about what they are most proud of, their results.

As for your second question: Having kids is part of saving the world. Where do you think the world comes from? :)"

-- Geoff Schmidt

text:
一图看懂 OpenAI 今天的 DevDay 发布了什么？主角绝对是 dots 👀 一种永远在线的 Agent，每个 dot 都有自己的云电脑和浏览器，按你定的目标 24 小时干活，还会主动推进任务，越用越懂你，现在就差 Anthropic 还没出 Personal Agent 了 ... dots 目前只开放给 Pro 和 Business Premium 用户。

模型这边发了 GPT-6.1 Sol，Agent Coding 和 Computer Use 接近 Astra，价格只要五分之一。还有一个 Ultrafast 速度档，在 Codex 里最快提速 8 倍，当然 API 价格也翻到 6 倍。OpenAI 为了它还专门出了 Pro 500 新订阅，用量是 Plus 的 25 倍。

开发者这边，Codex 被搬上了云端，在手机上就能派活、盯进度。Decisions API 让企业把重复的小决策交给 AI，但 AI 只能在给定的选项里选，Jev 直接被抄了，感觉它的使命结束了😅 Agents API 现在也能直接操作电脑了，OpenAI 还和 AWS 一起做了 Bedrock 托管 Agent。

真正的野心在 ChatGPT Space！你的团队和 dots 可在同一个空间里一起工作，再加上 Pages、Slides 和会议纪要，ChatGPT 越来越像 Slack + Notion + Drive 的合体。另外新推出 Sign in with ChatGPT，可以让你的订阅额度直接用在 Notion、Vercel 等 16 家产品里。

企业端有 OpenAI Marketplace，已有的 OpenAI 合同承诺额可以抵扣 Adobe、Figma、Salesforce、Harvey、CrowdStrike 等 32 家以上合作伙伴的软件费用！

我对 OpenAI 新产品路线的三点看法：

1. Dots 加 Space 意味着 OpenAI 在正面争夺「AI 员工」这个入口；

2. Sign in with ChatGPT 和 Marketplace 在把 ChatGPT 订阅变成一种跨应用的「货币」和分发渠道，第三方 SaaS 正在沦为 OpenAI 的 Token 分销商，并完全卷入 OpenAI 的生态；

3. 定价结构明显在往高端分层走：Pro 500 定位最高端，Ultrafast 按 6 倍价格收费，$200 档的用量被下调。这说明算力成本和 ARPU 压力仍是前沿 AI 公司的核心命题。

模型越来越便宜，但订阅越来越贵，模型公司都在避免自己被商品化，用平台生态来提升自己的护城河🤔

text:
In the AI-doomer argument, broad multidisciplinary thinkers like @sapinker have suggested the "kill-us-all" scenarios are preposterous. The AI researchers, that are most negatively outspoken, say that their voice should count more, because they are closest to AI and know what it can do.

Everyone watching this debate should read about Tetlock's work (see below). The generalists (foxes) and much better predictors than the specialists (hedgehogs) who are to close to the problem to accurately predict broader implications. 

So "no points" for the "we know more" argument. In fact, it works against you.
author: kevinnbass
quoted_text:
“One of the main lessons to come out of Tetlock’s work is that the best generalist forecasters are usually better at telling the future than domain-specific experts, even when it comes to those experts’ areas of study. This is because forecasting itself is its own science that requires a unique way of thinking, and a person having a great deal of knowledge about a field is no guarantee that they have good epistemological habits. If you’re going to ask, for example, whether American democracy is falling apart, an expert might start by making a superficial comparison between the modern US and the Weimar Republic. Someone with a forecasting mindset would be more likely to begin with a question like “how often do advanced democracies slide into dictatorships?” The answer is not very often.”

Important reminder from @RichardHanania that domain experts are not the best at predicting what happens, even in their own domains.

text:
OpenAI 推出 Decisions API：给 AI 出选择题，150 毫秒就可给出结果

OpenAI 在今天的开发者大会上发布了 Decisions API。开发者写好一个问题和几个备选答案，再把内容发过去，模型直接从选项里挑一个返回，不生成多余的内容。目前是有限预览，只对部分 API 客户开放，OpenAI 说未来几天会全面放开。

它用的是 GPT-6 家族里最小、最便宜的 Luna 的特化版本。按 OpenAI 的说法，一次判断大约 150 毫秒，同样的任务走普通 Luna 接口要 1.6 秒左右，快了十倍。

这类活儿以前有两种做法。一种是让大模型自由回答，再从一堆文字里解析结果，慢，还偶尔答非所问。另一种是专门训练一个分类器，得先攒标注数据，类别一变就要重训。Decisions API 把答案限定在你给的选项里，不可能跑出范围，换选项也只是改一下请求。

典型用法：客服工单进来，连同“账单组、技术组、售后组”几个候选一起发过去，马上知道该派给谁；内容审核时判断一张图能不能放行；AI 智能体每走一步，决定下一步调哪个工具。输入支持文字和图片。

不过社交媒体都在调侃 Decisions API 是在山寨 Jev。Jev 是创业公司 TypeSafe（创始人之一 Diogo Almeida）九月中旬发布的“决策模型”。普通聊天模型是一个字一个字往外生成，Jev 不生成文字，一次性给所有选项打分，直接返回答案和概率。TypeSafe 管它叫“System 1 模型”，借用心理学里“快思考”的说法：不推理，不解释，凭直觉秒答。

Jev 上线后在开发者圈很快传开。演示里有人一小时内就搭出能玩 Minecraft、Subway Surfers 的机器人，只要列出可选动作，不用训练。不过这些演示都跑在模拟器里，真实硬件上还没验证。它的价格也极低：输入每百万 token 0.042 美元，输出免费，处理一百万张三道判断题的工单大约 19 美元。

但细节上还是有差异： Jev 只收文本，Decisions API 能看图。Jev 每个答案都附带校准过的概率，方便设阈值，比如“低于 0.7 就转人工”，OpenAI 这边也会返回置信度。

text:
There is no good reason for mosquitoes to exist in wealthy countries today.

New technologies can get rid of the mosquito species that cause diseases like dengue, yellow fever, and malaria; and others can prevent them from carrying those diseases.
https://t.co/CddUFByGZA

So why do mosquitoes still exist? 

In a new article for Works in Progress, Maya Rosen explains how state incapacity and risk aversion led to over a decade of delays and billions of unnecessary bites in the United States.

Oxitec, for example, engineered an Aedes aegypti mosquito in such a way that its female offspring would die before adulthood. Through sustained releases, they showed they could reduce local mosquito populations by 80% or more, in field trials.

They sought approval from the USDA in 2010, which then passed it to the FDA, which passed it to the EPA. In 2020, the EPA allowed them to conduct limited field trials in the Florida Keys. Two years ago, their experimental permit expired, and they still need another review before it can be used routinely. Their proposed field trial in California was withdrawn after public opposition.

Another company, MosquitoMate, developed a technique involving Wolbachia, which also suppresses local mosquitoes. They then spent over fifteen years working through the system before finally receiving commercial registration nationwide in 2024.

It seems that, sometimes, the barrier to getting rid of diseases isn’t technology at all. It’s policy and political will.

New products shouldn’t get stuck in regulatory review for so long, especially if the delays are about basic questions like which agency has oversight over the product, rather than testing for safety.

Though some of those uncertainties were being addressed, the broader changes haven’t materialized. After Biden’s 2022 executive order, the agencies planned to update how their coordinated framework was implemented. But Trump rescinded the order last year.

Meanwhile, the EPA unit that reviews new mosquito control products is still a small office backlogged in reviewing a wide range of products.

Mosquitoes are a policy choice. We can get rid of them. Will we choose to?
https://t.co/CddUFByGZA

text:
The Trump coin gets called a fiasco almost every time it comes up. I don't agree, and I say that as someone who traded it.

Here's what that label skips. In about two days its total valuation went from roughly

$200 million

to about

$75 billion

For a trader, that was about as good as a short trade gets. I can't think of a coin that ran that hard that fast.

Yes, it bled for a long time after. That's what meme coins do. They go up a lot, then they go down for a very long time.

I didn't get in under a billion. My entry was at a valuation of around

$2 billion

and it was still a decent bag. So I'm not going to tell you nobody made money on it. I did, and a lot of traders did too.

Now, if you bought in the first week after the top, yes, you were down fast. That part is real. But you can't look at that chart and say the people trading it didn't benefit.

Compare that with the meme coins whose very first trade was already priced near the top. It didn't matter how early you were. They never went up at all, so nobody early got paid.

That's the real difference, and it's the part I care about as a trader. A meme coin launch should be judged by where it starts and where you got in.

Think about it this way. If you got into a coin at 100 million and it ran 20x, are you going to be sad about that, even if it goes down after? That's the view I come from.

To be clear, I wouldn't touch the Trump coin now. It's been slowly bleeding ever since. But saying it only took people's money isn't true, and the chart shows it

My take on the whole Near privacy vs permissioned drama: 

We have had hardcore cypherpunk systems in crypto for decades. That has been the entire ethos of this industry, and they has taken us this far. 

We have the fruits of that experiment.
We also have the scars, too. 

Incredible amounts of lost funds, North Korean exploits, user harm, etc. 

A new experiment, one where we can discern between good and bad and take action as a result, is worth having. 

Spare me the slippery slope of "but all our freedoms will be threatened!"

We still have the maximally permissionless systems too - you can use those.

text:
Impressive. This set of talks, along with the new America dot gov website, has the unmistakable feel of an Apple launch event. They're rebooting the federal government as a tech startup. Several observations.

(1) First, with this new AI interface to the entire federal government, if it works as promised, there won't be a single American who can't say their life wasn't helped at least in part by AI, or that the benefits accrued solely to zillionaires. This in itself cannily mitigates anti-datacenter sentiment.

(2) Second, Joe Gebbia and Marco Rubio's talks on simplifying name changes and passport filings introduce a completely new era where the US government is actually launching tangible features that benefit users.

(3) Third, this launch event in and of itself may visibly drive reform. It could become much more important than the State of the Union. Unlike laws, code is user-visible, and can be instantly audited by the public, as Obama found out with the failed obamacare website launch. So: the annual America dot gov event may be substance, whereas SOTU is traditionally optics. I wouldn't be surprised to see the President present at the next one.

(4) Fourth, this kind of event is a perfect example of where tech and red cooperate best. They both hate bureaucracy. Automating paperwork with code reduces the power of statists over both capitalists and nationalists. It's also hard to undo by other admins: once you digitize a process, hard to turn it back to paper.

(5) Fifth, it's an obvious point perhaps, but think about how much influence YCombinator has had in 20 years. From Gebbia's Airbnb joining their 2009 batch to a complete overhaul of the user interface of the US bureaucracy, and thus the US government.

(6) Sixth, this is another take on the network state. The functional part of the US (the network, meaning tech) is merging with and partially reforming the dysfunctional part (the state, meaning bureaucracy) by automating 20th century paper forms.

As a tech startup, there will no doubt be bugs and user issues and so on, but unlike with paper laws those issues will be visible and the code fixes will be verifiable. A new era of AI America. Rooting for them.
